title: Credentials Exposed in HTML Comments
description: The homepage contains hardcoded test credentials (test1:test1) exposed in an HTML comment with a TODO reminder to remove them. The credentials are visible in the page source to any user who views the page, making them susceptible to unauthorized access. This represents a critical security misconfiguration where sensitive information is exposed in plain text within the client-side visible HTML.
impact: An attacker can view the page source and extract the test credentials to gain unauthorized access to the application. Even though these appear to be test credentials, they should never be visible in production code or comments. This violates security best practices and can lead to unauthorized access if these credentials are actually valid. Additionally, the presence of TODO comments indicates incomplete security remediation.
evidence:
POC Execution Output:
- Command: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/
- Vulnerability: CONFIRMED - Credentials found in HTML comments
- Extracted credentials: <!-- test1:test1 TODO: remove-->
- Location: In the HTML head/body section, visible in page source
- Context: The credentials appear in an HTML comment with a developer TODO note

Full context from the response:
```
</head>
<body>
    <!-- test1:test1 TODO: remove-->
    <form action="/login" method="post">
        <input type="text" name="username" placeholder="Username" required>
```

The POC script successfully detected and extracted these credentials, proving that any user can access this information by viewing the page source.
remediation:
1. Remove all hardcoded credentials from HTML comments and source code immediately
2. Implement a credential management system using environment variables or secure vaults for any test/demo credentials
3. Never include TODO comments about removing credentials - remove them immediately before deployment
4. Use code review and linting tools (e.g., GitGuardian, Truffleog, detect-secrets) to detect exposed credentials before deployment
5. Implement pre-commit hooks to prevent commits with credentials in code
6. Conduct a comprehensive security audit to identify any other hardcoded credentials in the codebase
7. Use secret scanning tools in your CI/CD pipeline to catch credential leaks automatically
8. If legitimate test credentials are needed, use a separate test environment with proper credential management
references: OWASP A02:2021 - Cryptographic Failures, CWE-798 - Use of Hard-Coded Credentials, CWE-215 - Information Exposure Through Debug Information, OWASP - Sensitive Data Exposure
